passthrough.title: Passthrough diagnostics
passthrough.intro: Run a guided check to find exactly where UART passthrough to the receiver fails.
passthrough.safety: Before running: props off and the aircraft on a bench. Passthrough energizes the flight controller and powers the receiver — confirm your wiring and make sure nothing can spin.
passthrough.success: Passthrough reached the receiver — a valid CRSF frame was seen.

failure.controllerNotResponding: The flight controller didn't answer MSP. Check the port and baud, and confirm Betaflight/iNav is running (not in DFU/bootloader).
failure.passthroughUnavailable: The controller is reachable but wouldn't enter serial passthrough. Update the flight-controller firmware or pick the correct UART.
failure.rxNotPowered: Passthrough opened but the receiver sent nothing back — it likely isn't powered. Check the receiver's 5V and GND.
failure.rxNotWired: Bytes came back, but not from a CRSF receiver on the selected UART — the receiver isn't wired to that UART. Re-check TX↔RX and the chosen port.
failure.crsfTimeout: The receiver is responding but no valid CRSF frame arrived in time — usually a baud mismatch. Try another baud.

explain.band24: 2.4 GHz gives lower latency and higher packet rates — the right trade-off for close-in flying.
explain.band900: 900 MHz travels farther and punches through obstacles better, which suits long-range flying.

recovery.checkUsb: Check the USB cable and that the device is powered.
recovery.reconnect: Unplug and reconnect the device, then retry.
recovery.bootloaderMode: Put the device into bootloader/flashing mode and retry.
recovery.installDriver: Install the USB-serial driver for your device.
recovery.checkPermissions: Make sure no other app is using the serial port.
recovery.linuxUdev: On Linux, add yourself to the dialout group or install the udev rules.
recovery.verifyTarget: Confirm you picked the correct brand and model.
recovery.verifyDeviceType: Make sure a TX firmware goes to a TX (and RX to an RX).
recovery.chooseAnotherVersion: Go back and choose a different firmware version — retrying this one won't help.
recovery.checkNetwork: Check your internet connection and try again.
recovery.retry: Wait a moment and try again.
recovery.deviceWifiMode: Confirm the device is in WiFi mode and reachable.
recovery.checkPlatformio: Confirm PlatformIO is installed and on your PATH.
recovery.installEsptool: Install esptool (pip install esptool) and make sure it's on your PATH, then try again.
recovery.configureFcUart: In Betaflight/iNav Configurator, set the UART the receiver is wired to as Serial RX, then save and reboot.
recovery.updateFcFirmware: Update the flight-controller firmware — older builds have no MSP serial passthrough.
recovery.flashOverUsb: Or wire the receiver straight to a USB-serial adapter and flash it over UART instead.
recovery.reflashDevice: Flash the device again with the same firmware before using it — don't rely on the firmware it had before.
recovery.keepDevicePowered: Keep the device connected and powered for the whole flash; don't unplug it while it's writing.
recovery.viewLog: Open the build log below for the full details.
recovery.reportIssue: If it persists, copy the diagnostic report and ask for help.

finding.explainAria: Ask Omnia to explain this finding
finding.rssiFloor: RSSI bottomed out at {{rssi}} dBm — the receiver was at its sensitivity floor.
finding.snrNoise: Noisy signal — SNR varied by ±{{stdDev}} dB over {{window}} samples.
finding.packetInstability: Unstable packet rate — {{changes}} rate changes within {{window}} samples.
finding.txPowerSaturation: TX power pinned at {{txPower}} mW while RSSI averaged {{avgRssi}} dBm — no power headroom left.

why.lqCollapse: A sudden link-quality drop means control packets stopped getting through — the moment most likely to precede a failsafe.
why.rssiFloor: At the noise floor the receiver can no longer separate signal from noise, so any further loss is an immediate dropout.
why.snrNoise: A jumpy signal-to-noise ratio points to interference or a marginal antenna path that erodes range and reliability.
why.packetInstability: A packet rate that keeps switching suggests the link is renegotiating under stress instead of holding a stable mode.
why.txPowerSaturation: Running at maximum power with a weak link means there is no headroom left to push through — you are already at the edge of range.

patternCheck.repeatedLqDrops: Repeated drops usually mean range or obstruction, not a one-off glitch — check antenna placement and fly a shorter range to confirm.
patternCheck.headingDegradation: A direction-linked null points at antenna orientation or the airframe blocking the signal — reposition the antenna or add diversity facing the weak sector.
patternCheck.gpsAreaDegradation: The same weak spot on every pass is environmental — note the location and avoid it, or gain altitude through it.
patternCheck.powerPacketLinkEvents: Power ramping into every drop means you are at the edge of the link budget — reduce range or step up the antenna/TX setup.

model.title: Model prototype (M58)
model.verdictFailed: This model did NOT clear the M56 ship gate. clearsM56Gate() returned false.
model.verdictCleared: This model cleared the M56 ship gate.
model.verdictReason: It could not. The v2.0 rule engine scores a false-positive rate of {{baselineFp}} on the same held-out sessions, and the gate requires a model to be strictly below the rule engine. Nothing is strictly below zero — so no model clears this gate, not this one and not a perfect one. The rules were also written against these very sessions, so their perfect score is a ceiling, not field performance: there is nothing here to beat.
model.dataBar: The model was fitted to {{rows}} healthy sessions. The data bar (D21) is {{required}} labeled sessions per class. Every number on this panel is indicative only — it is not a gate pass, and this prototype reaches no user.

scores.caption: The model prototype and the deterministic v2.0 rule engine, scored on the same sessions
scores.quantum: The held-out set has {{negatives}} healthy sessions, so its false-positive rate can only move in {{quantum}}-point steps — it has four possible values and nothing in between. A rate computed on three sessions is not a measurement, and it must not be read as one.

model.advisoryNote: The model is advisory only. It never writes device configuration or firmware, it never changes a diagnostic finding, and its output stays on this device.

predictive.title: Predictive failsafe warning (M59) — experiment
predictive.verdictFailed: This experiment did NOT meet its acceptance. It is research-only, and it is NOT a validated feature.
predictive.verdictMet: This experiment met its acceptance on the real corpus.
predictive.verdictReason: It could not. The question M59 asked was "can we warn a pilot before the link dies?". On OmniLink's real reference flights the answer is no. In {{zeroLead}} of the {{events}} recorded link losses the link gives literally zero warning — quality falls from healthy to zero in a single 40 ms sample. Across all of them, the most warning ANY predictor could possibly extract is {{oracleMax}} ms, and the typical amount is {{oracleMedian}} ms. The target is {{target}} ms. There is no early-warning signal in the data to find.
predictive.nullCeiling: Best case for any predictor: {{oracleMax}} ms of warning (typical: {{oracleMedian}} ms) against a {{target}} ms target.
predictive.nullCeilingNote: This is a ceiling on what is possible, not a score this predictor achieved. It is measured from the recorded flights alone, with no model involved — so a better model cannot beat it.
predictive.nullPredictor: This predictor warned ahead of {{predicted}} of the {{events}} recorded link losses. It caught {{late}} only after the link was already gone, and missed {{missed}} entirely.
predictive.nullLate: Catching a link loss after it happens is detection, not prediction — and OmniLink's existing alerts already do that.
predictive.syntheticTitle: On drawn test data (not real flights)
predictive.syntheticWarning: The numbers below come from {{sessions}} sessions a generator DREW, not from real flights. They were drawn alongside this predictor, with degradation ramps deliberately made long enough that a {{target}} ms warning is available at all. They show the code runs. They are NOT evidence that it would work in the air, and they are NOT an acceptance pass.
predictive.syntheticLead: On the drawn ramps it warns {{median}} ms ahead, on average.
predictive.syntheticFalseAlarms: But it also raises a false alarm on {{falseAlarms}} of {{negatives}} drawn sessions that dipped and RECOVERED — including {{deepFalseAlarms}} of {{deepNegatives}} where the link nearly died and came back.
predictive.syntheticTension: That is not a flaw to be fixed. Until the moment a link actually dies, a flight that recovers and a flight that does not look identical. Buying early warning means buying the false alarms that come with it.
predictive.safetyTitle: If this ever ships, read this first
predictive.safety: A predictive warning is a guess about the near future, not a measurement of the present. It can be wrong in both directions: it can warn when nothing is about to happen, and it can stay silent right up until the link is gone. It cannot be relied upon to keep an aircraft in the air, it does not replace your own judgement about range and line of sight, and it never changes anything on your hardware.
predictive.prototype: Unvalidated prototype. On OmniLink's real reference flights this predictor found no early-warning signal at all. Nothing here is enabled for normal users.
